solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Somewhere to buy drinks from yard

blocks.note: 'off' can mean away from, as in 'off the shelf'
Y is the standard abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: Someone collects drinks from a merchant's yard.
explanation.walkthrough: An offy is British slang for an off-licence, a shop licensed to sell alcohol for drinking elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Offy is informal British shorthand for an off-licence, a liquor shop.

clue.text: E.g. scorpion's belly poisons moth without number fluttering on one

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking, so a letter is taken away
something fluttering moves erratically, so the letters are jumbled
in a down entry, 'on' puts the jumble above the final piece

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for number
one is a

explanation.surface: A scorpion's abdomen holds poisons for a fluttering moth.
explanation.walkthrough: N is dropped from POISONS MOTH, the remaining ten letters are rearranged, and A is added at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The opisthosoma is the rear body section of arachnids such as scorpions, their abdomen.

clue.text: Start of hole in tooth causing anxiety

indicators.note: 'in' places the first piece inside the second

blocks.note: a fang is a long pointed tooth
in golf each hole begins from the tee

explanation.surface: The beginnings of a cavity in a tooth make a patient nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of hole' tempts you to take the letter H; it is the golf tee.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanteeg is a dialect word for a state of fuss or anxiety.

clue.text: Note Mac's ball comes in – it's not appropriate for wicket

indicators.note: something that comes in enters the other word and sits inside it

blocks.note: a fiver is a five-pound note
ba' is the Scots word for ball; Mac stands for a Scot

explanation.surface: A cricketer's ball arrives, but it is the wrong thing for the wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: Wicket suggests cricket; it is a small gate. A five-bar gate is a large field gate, not a wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: Five-bar describes a large field gate with five bars, unlike a wicket, which is a small pedestrian gate.

clue.text: Lung infection about over – it lasts a very long time

definitions.text: it lasts a very long time

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: SARS is severe acute respiratory syndrome
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A respiratory illness may be over, but its effects linger for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls, written O on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: A saros is the eclipse cycle of about eighteen years, a lengthy astronomical period.

clue.text: Glittering Scotch stuff – secretive about that

indicators.note: 'about' places one word round the other, wrapping it on both sides

blocks.note: sly means furtive or secretive
in Scots, to pang is to stuff or cram

explanation.surface: A sparkling Scottish fabric is being discussed by someone who keeps their own counsel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' points back to the Scotch stuff: the secretive word goes around it, giving S-PANG-LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Spangly describes something covered in spangles, small shiny discs, so glittering is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Time to take exam, hard

blocks.note: to sit an exam is to take it
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: It's time to take an exam, and a difficult one.
explanation.walkthrough: Sith is an obsolete word from Chambers; in one old sense it means times or occasions.
explanation.definitionFit: Sith is an archaic noun for an occasion or time, related to the word since.

clue.text: Abbot's equivalent offering religious teaching with love crowd embraces

indicators.note: a crowd that embraces something holds it within its arms

blocks.note: a press is a dense crowd
RI is religious instruction in British schools
love is zero in tennis, O

explanation.surface: An abbot's counterpart preaches lovingly while a crowd surrounds her.
explanation.walkthrough: RI, religious instruction, is a British school subject; love is the tennis score nought.
explanation.definitionFit: A prioress heads a priory of nuns, the female counterpart of an abbot or prior.

clue.text: No belly flop? I do seven, floundering

indicators.note: something floundering struggles clumsily, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A diver boasts of doing seven clean dives without a single belly flop.
explanation.walkthrough: A belly flop lands flat on the stomach; the opposite is a steep dive head first.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosedive goes in head first and steeply, the very opposite of a flat belly flop.

clue.text: Angy suffering with a spot of eczema – in this specialist department?

indicators.note: a spot is just a small amount, so only the opening letter is taken
suffering letters are in distress and twisted out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Angie, suffering from a patch of eczema, wonders if this is the right hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: Angy reads as a misspelt name; it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Gynae is British shorthand for gynaecology, the hospital department for women's health.

clue.text: Non-professional, i.e. amateur, I'll appear in left centre

indicators.note: things that appear in something show up inside it

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
A is a standard abbreviation for amateur
the speaker, I, is the one who will appear
C is an abbreviation for centre

explanation.surface: An amateur sportsman boasts he will feature at left centre.
explanation.walkthrough: A and I go between L and C.
explanation.definitionFit: Laic means of the laity, not clergy or professional, so a non-professional or layman.

clue.text: Couple of queens or a threesome?

blocks.note: a couple is a pair
queens are royal, so something of queens is royal

explanation.surface: Is it a pair of queens or a party of three?
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay seems to describe two cards, yet the card-game term it builds means three of a kind, so 'couple' and 'threesome' clash amusingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pair royal is a card-game term for a set of three matching cards, such as three queens.

clue.text: Bookish person

blocks.note: surface: someone fond of reading
setter's reading: a person who works with books as a professional writer or critic

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a bare definition with no wordplay at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A littérateur is a literary man of letters, devoted to writing and reading books.

clue.text: Sugary enzyme contained in blood vessel, right inside

indicators.note: 'inside' places the abbreviation within the blood vessel word

blocks.note: something contained is in
a vein carries blood to the heart
RT is an abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A sweet enzyme is found in the bloodstream, on the right side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contained' reads as part of the surface but supplies the opening two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Invertin, also called invertase, is the enzyme that splits cane sugar into glucose and fructose.

clue.text: Secretary in US office inundated by post – enough!

indicators.note: something inundated is submerged by the words that follow, sitting buried within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An American office worker is swamped by mail and finally cries 'Enough!'
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and exclamation hide that the answer straddles po-ST ENO-ugh.
explanation.definitionFit: Steno is American shorthand for a stenographer, an office worker taking dictation.

clue.text: One entertained in clergyman's home (briefly) has to behave

indicators.note: 'briefly' asks for the word to be cut short, here losing its ending
a guest entertained in a house is inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: one is a, the indefinite article
a rector lives in a rectory

explanation.surface: A guest staying at the vicarage must mind their manners.
explanation.walkthrough: RECTORY is abbreviated to RECT, and A sits inside it: RE(A)CT.
explanation.definitionFit: To react is to act or respond in a certain way, which is to behave.

clue.text: Resentment about wretch getting trading licence

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: pique is wounded pride or resentment
a rat is a despicable person

explanation.surface: Resentment arises when a scoundrel gets a trading permit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a maritime term: a ship needs it before trading at a port.
explanation.definitionFit: Pratique is permission given to a ship to trade with a port after quarantine is cleared.

clue.text: Harsh tax north of the border about clear

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the tax word wraps round the other

blocks.note: stent is a Scottish word for a tax or assessment; north of the border means Scotland
to clear a place of something is to rid it

explanation.surface: A harsh tax in Scotland is all about clearing debts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North of the border' means Scotland, telling you the tax word is Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Strident means loud and grating, so a harsh sound or tone is strident.

clue.text: The in-crowd attempts to grasp ambition

indicators.note: to grasp something is to hold it within, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: tries are attempts
an end is a goal or aim

explanation.surface: The fashionable set strive to seize their goals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ambition' is the goal one aims at, the sense of an end in view.
explanation.definitionFit: Trendies are fashionable people, the clique that is in with current style.

clue.text: One in suit showing the human body back to front

indicators.note: the letter at the back of the word moves round to the front

blocks.note: earth can mean the human body, the mortal clay of the soul

explanation.surface: A tailor's suit displays the body reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: The final letter of EARTH moves to the start. A heart is a card in the suit of hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: Any card of the hearts suit is called a heart, so it is one member of that suit.

clue.text: Call at table sent back, tucked into cooked eel, nourishing

indicators.note: a word sent back is read in the opposite direction
cooked food is altered, so these letters are reworked
tucked into means placed inside the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
at the bridge table, each call is a bid

explanation.surface: A diner returns a dish of cooked eel, though it was quite wholesome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call at table' looks like summoning a waiter; it is a bridge call.
explanation.definitionFit: Edible means fit to be eaten, so food that is edible can nourish you.

clue.text: Give a ticking-off for singular mess

indicators.note: making a plural word singular drops its final plural ending

blocks.note: a bollocks is British slang for a mess or botch

explanation.surface: Someone is told off for making a single mess.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a bollocks is a botched job, and to bollock someone is to reprimand them severely.
explanation.definitionFit: To bollock is coarse British slang for giving someone a severe reprimand.

clue.text: Some African tin, curiously tensile

indicators.note: done curiously means done in an odd way, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Some African tin turns out to be oddly stretchy.
explanation.walkthrough: Tin is old slang for money, not the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisente is the plural of sente, small coins of Lesotho, so some African money.

clue.text: Raged wildly after bottom mark in 4th-year exam? (6, two words)

indicators.note: acting wildly is acting out of order, so the letters are rearranged
'after' places the rearranged word behind the mark

blocks.note: the lowest possible mark is nought, O
the letters of raged rearranged

explanation.surface: A pupil flew into a rage on getting zero in a fourth-year exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The O grade was the Scottish exam formerly taken in the fourth year of secondary school.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish pupils sat O grade exams around the fourth year of secondary school, before Standard grades replaced them.

clue.text: System for weighing left page caught in publicity

indicators.note: something caught in is trapped inside the other word

blocks.note: to give something air is to publicise it
VO, verso, is the left-hand page of an open book

explanation.surface: A weighing method was mentioned on the left page of a promotional leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: Verso is the printing term for a left-hand page, abbreviated in two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Avoir is a short form of avoirdupois, the system of weights based on the pound of sixteen ounces.

clue.text: What chord may be, but roughly dividing opinion

indicators.note: done roughly means done in a messy, disordered way, so the word is rearranged
something dividing another splits it, so it sits in the middle

blocks.note: the sense of a meeting is its general opinion
the letters of but rearranged

explanation.surface: A musical chord may be all that's needed, though it splits listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chord' suggests music; here it is the geometry chord, a line joining two points on a curve.
explanation.definitionFit: A subtense is a line that subtends an arc or angle, and a chord does exactly that.

clue.text: Liquors (Scotch) making pound by the sound of it

indicators.note: the answer is judged by how it is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: to pound is to batter, which leaves bruises

explanation.surface: Scotch liquor makes a pounding noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Broo is Scots for broth or liquor, the liquid food is cooked in.
explanation.definitionFit: Broos is the Scots plural of broo, meaning broth or cooking liquor.

clue.text: Heads for the Levant, food containing hint of spice

indicators.note: a hint is a trace, so only the first letter is kept
'containing' means holding the other piece inside

blocks.note: eats is informal for food
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Travellers make for the Middle East, with food flavoured with spices.
explanation.walkthrough: Heads looks like a noun; it is the verb, moving towards. The Levant is the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: To east is to move eastwards, so someone heading to the Levant easts.

clue.text: Iris, not the character to lead in folk dance

indicators.note: the leading character, the first letter, is to be left off

blocks.note: morris is the traditional English folk dance with bells and sticks

explanation.surface: Iris is not the person to lead the folk dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris looks like a woman's name; it is the plant. MORRIS loses its M.
explanation.definitionFit: Orris is a kind of iris, whose root is dried for perfume.

clue.text: I make a mess of turning up garment made of oriental material

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means reading from the bottom

blocks.note: I then mar, to spoil or make a mess of

explanation.surface: Someone ruins a garment made from eastern fabric by turning it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' sounds like hemming a garment; it reverses I MAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Rami is a variant of ramie, an East Asian plant fibre woven into cloth.

clue.text: Wager soldier maybe placed on ending of warfare

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter alone
in a down entry, being placed on puts one piece above the other

blocks.note: a soldier is one caste of ant
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bet on a soldier surviving the end of the war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldier maybe' points to a soldier ant, one kind of the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An ante is a stake put into the pot before cards are dealt, a wager.

clue.text: Ornamental tag made of silver, an impediment?

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a let is an obstruction, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A decorative tag made of silver turns out to be a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: Let in its old sense is a hindrance, still heard in tennis and legal phrases.
explanation.definitionFit: An aglet is the metal tag on the end of a lace, often decorative.

clue.text: Mineral dioxide preserves depth of colour

blocks.note: food is preserved by canning it, so to tin is to preserve
tone is the shade or depth of a colour

explanation.surface: A mineral compound keeps its rich colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preserves' looks like a verb joining the parts; it is a verb supplying the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinstone, or cassiterite, is the ore of tin, tin dioxide.

clue.text: SA chap involved in disturbed matter with English, a minor affair

indicators.note: something disturbed is thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged
involved in means wrapped up inside the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English
ou is South African slang for a man or chap

explanation.surface: A South African man caught up in a troubled English matter has a little fling.
explanation.walkthrough: Ou is South African slang for a man, a favourite of Azed's.
explanation.definitionFit: An amourette is a petty love affair, a diminutive of amour.

clue.text: She entertains, putting energy into being careless

indicators.note: putting something into another places it inside

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
disuse is the state of being neglected, uncared for

explanation.surface: A performer injects energy into seeming carefree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting ... into' is split around 'energy'. Disuse is neglect, the condition of something no one cares for.
explanation.definitionFit: A diseuse is a female performer of monologues, so she entertains audiences.

clue.text: Will's beetle we released from prong?

indicators.note: letters released from a word are let go, removed from it

blocks.note: taken as written
a skewer is a pointed prong for meat

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's beetle is set free from a spike.
explanation.walkthrough: Will is Shakespeare; his sker, to scurry or scour about, is the verb beetle. SKEWER loses WE.
explanation.definitionFit: To beetle is to scurry, and sker is a Shakespearean verb for scurrying or scouring along.
